As far as this Ministry is aware, certain rules/directions
have been issued by the State Governments of U. P., Karnataka,
Maharashtra, Mizoram and the Union Territories of Delhi and
Chandigarh so as to require compulsory wearing of crash hel-
mets by the drivers and in certain cases by the pillion riders also.

As indicated above Parliament has passed the legislation to
require the drivers as well as the pillion riders to wear crash
helmets. The question of appointment of any Committee or
body for the purpose therefore does not arise. Further, in this
context the furnishing of justification for making such manda-
tory requirement by this Ministry does not arise. It is well
known that the measure is for protection against likely head in-
jury if any accident occurs. This is a road safety measure. The
number of accidents involving only the scooters and pillion
riders for the last three years are not readily available.

In this regard, it may further be stated that a Committee on
Road safety was appointed by the Government, which submitted
its report to Government in 1972. The Committee had recom-
mended that in a majority of cases, the drivers/riders of the two
wheeled vehicles die as a result of head injuries. The Com-
mittee had recommended eventually amendment of the Act to
make it compulsory for the drivers/riders to wear crash helmets

(Para 90 of Chapter 8 of the Report). After considering the re-
commendations, the Act was amended by Parliament.

Section 85A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, as inserted in
1977 also enables the Central Government to provide for such
exceptions as it may think fit by the rules to be framed by it.
The provisions of the Act inserted in 1977 and the rules notified
vide GSR No. 261(E) of 1980, are to become effective w.e.f 1st
November, 1980.

Representations had been received from the Shiromini
Gurudwara Parbandhak Committee, Amritsar as well as its
Delhi Unit urging upon the Government to exempt Sikh ladies
also from wearing crash helmets as it was against their religious
feelings A deputation of Sikh leaders including Shri Tohra,
President SGPC and Shri Talwandi, President Akali Dal had
met the former Minister of State (Shri Chand Ram) on 17-5-
1973. It wes explained to them that it was a safety measure
@nd the Sikh ledies in their own interest could also wear crash
helmets. However, they imsisied upon the exemption on the
ground that such a course would be against their religious tenets.



&
As they continued to insist upon this, the then Minister for
Shipping and Transport decided that the Sikh ladies may be
given exemption under the rules io be framed by the Central
Government. Accordingly, the Sikh ladies have been given
exemption under the rules notified by the Government. These
rules, have, however, been finalised after getting it approved
from the present Minister for Shipping and Transport.
This issues with the appiuval of Joint Secretary (T).”
9. On a question being asked whether there was any proposal to
exempt all women and children below 12 from the operation of the
rules, the Ministry simply stated that they had no proposal under
consideration to exempt all pillion riders from the mandatory require-
ment of wearing a helmet.

10. At its sitting held on the 9th October, 1980, the Committee
again considered the rules in the light of the comments furnished by
the Ministry and desired to be informed about the provision under
which male Sikhs had been exempted from the requirement of
wearing crash helmets and the practice obtaining in the U.K. in
relation to such Sikhs. The Commttee also decided to hear the
representatives of the Ministries of Shipping and Transport and Law
on the point.

वा. The Ministry sent the following information in compliance
with the Committee’s above direction:—
(i) The provision under which male Sikhs stand exempted from
wearing crash helmets while driving scooters, etc.

First proviso to Section 85(A) inserted by Act No. 27 of
1977 provides for exemption of male Sikhs from wearing crash
helmets while driving or riding on ‘the motor-cycle, in a publie
place, wearing a turban. This is to be brought into force wie
effect from 1st November, 1980 vide Notification No. TGM-
78-I dated 14th May, 1980.

(ii) Practice obtaining in the U.K. in this regard

While the precise details as of today are not available, it had
earlier in 1977 been brought to our notice that Sikhs wearing
turbans are exempted from wearing of crash helmets while
riding two-wheeler motor vehicles. It would however be rele-
vant to mention that due to climatic conditions the two-wheelers
scooters are not much in vogue in the U.K.

12. The Committee at its sitting held on the 21st October, 1980,

heard the representatives of the Ministries of Shipping and Trans-
port (Transport Wing) and Law (Department of Legal Affairs).



=|

13. The Committee initially took objection to the provision made
in rules exempting Sikh women from the operation of section 85A
of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The representatives of the Ministry
of Shipping and Transport explained that that provision was being
made on the analogy of the exemption granted under the Act to male
Sikhs. They also informed the Committee that the exemption from

putting on protective headgear was proposed to be extended to all
women and children below the age of 12 years.

14..The Committee is not in favour of exemption being given from
the requirement of section 85A so liberally, particularly, in view of
the fact that that requirement is inteneded as a safety measure. The
Committee, therefore, fels that Government should keep in view
that aspect before considering grant of any exemption and also care-
fully consider the validity of such exemptions in the light of the pro~
visions contained in articles 14, 15 and 16 of the Constitution,

REGULATIONS MADE UNDER THE MAJOR PORT TRUSTS
ACT, 1963

15. Sections 28, 123, 124, 126 and 132 of the Major Port Trusts
Act, 1963, deal with making and publication of regulations under the

Act.

A reading of the above mentioned provisions makes it clear that
the initial regulations, relating to the service conditions and other
matters of the employees and for the efficient and proper adminis-
‘tration of a major port are required to be made by the Central Gov-
ernment and published in the Gazette of India. Subsequent amend-
ments to such regulations are made by the Board of Trustees of the
concerned port and published only in ‘the Official Gazette of the
State in which that port is situated. Consequently, amendments
made to regulations by ‘the Board of Trustees, though approved by

the Central Government, escape the scrutiny of the Committee on
Subordinate Legislation.

The regulations made under the authority of a Board could be
brought within the purview of the Committee if a provision was
incorporated in the Act making laying of every regulation made
under the Act before each House of Parliament, obligatory.

16. The Committee considered the matter at its meeting held on
the 11th November, 1980, with a view to bringing the regulations



6

i. the authority of a Board within its purview. The Com-
mittee directs that a provision should be incorporated in the Major

- Port Trusts Act, 1963, to the effect that every regulation made under
the Act, as Soon as may be afer it is made, be laid before each House

of Parliament while it is in session. Till such provision
is incorporated in the Act, Government should on its own take the

initiative to lay such regulations on the Table of each House of
Parliament. ie

| Himachal Pradesh Government were accordingly addressed in the

matter and their replies are as follows:—

“....that this Ministry is unable to appreciate the alleged

discrepancy referred to in your Office Memorandum. In _ this

Ministry’s letter dated the 26th May, 1980, it haq been stated

that 40 eligible EACs of Hima*hal Pradesh were considered for

j ; inclusion in the initial constitution of Delhi and Himachal Pra-
if desh Civil Service. Out of those 40 officers, 26 officers were
found suit*ble by the Selection Committee for initial appoint-

ment to the service and the remaining 14 officers were not found

Suitable for such appointment. In Shri K. N. Dhulap’s letter,



25

he mentioned about 17 officers, these 17 officers included only
6 of 14 officers who were considered by the Selection Committee
and not found suitable for initial appointment. The remaining
11 officers were not eligible for initial appointment and were
therefore not considered by the Selection Committee. A state-
ment indicating the position of these 17 officers was forwarded
with this Ministry’s letter wherein the position of these officers
was clearly explained.

In view of the circumstances mentioneg above, there is no
discrepancy involved. It is, therefore, requested that the Pposi-
tion may kindly be made clear to the Members of the Committee
on Subordinate Legislation,”

[O.M, dated 21-6-1980 from the Ministry of Home Affairs]

“...that the Himachal Pradesh Government is concerned
with the following two recommendations of Rajya Sabha Com-
mittee on Subordinate Legislation made in its 37th Report: —

(i) To regularise the Select-list Officers of defunct
DHANICS who are still working as such in HPAS; and

(ii) To count continuous service rendered by a member
of the HPAS prior to his appointment to the said service
under rule 15, as a Select List Officer of the defunct
DHANICS for the award of Selection Grade of HPAS.

So far as the first recommendation is concerned, necessary
amendment to this effect has already been made in the HPAS
Rules, 1973 vide this Government Not'fication No. PER (A-I)-B
(15)-2/79 dated the 29th December, 1979 as already intimated to
you in detail vide this Government letter of even number dated
the 8th January, 1980. The cases of all the Select-list Officers
of defunct DHANICS presently officiating in HPAS purely on
temporary basis have already been sent to the H:P. Public Ser-
vice Commission and the Commission has fixed a meeting of
D.P.C. for 18-8-1980 to consider the regularisation of these

* Officers,

As to the second recommendation the position is that the
HPAS/HPPS Rules have been amended to the following extent
as per recommendations of the Rajya Sabha Committee on Sub-
ordinate Legislation, vide this Department Notifications No.
8-176/71-DP (Apptt.) I.dated the 26th May, 1980 and Notification
No. Karmik (A+1)-B (7)-2/79 dated the 2nd June, 1980 (Annexure
VI & VI):— .



26

“Provided that the continuous service rendered by a
member of the HPAS/HPPS prior to his appointment to the
said service under rule 14-15 as a Select List Officer of the
defunct DHANICS/DHANIPS against duty posts of
DHANICS-DHANIPS/HPAS/HPPS/such _ex-cadre posts,

taken into account for determining the length of service
for the award of Selection Grade of the said Service.”

In so far as the release of Selection Grade according to these
amendments, is concerned, it is stated for information that some
direct recruit of HPAS have filed a Civil Suit in the Court of
Chief Judicial Magistrate, Simla challenging the above referred
amendment which is still pending for decision, Simultaneously
they have also put in representations claiming that if the junior
officers according to these amendments become eligible for the
award of selection grade then all the seniors to him shall also
be considered for the award of selection grade. This entire
matter is under examination of this Government.

Regarding other recommendations of the Committee i.e. to
count the service rendereg by these officers as Select List Officers
of defunct DHANICS/EAC etc. for promotion to IAS and to
consider them for promotion to the IAS by relaxing their age
limit, tae H.P. Government is not concerned with these recom-
mendations. These pertain to the Department of Personnel,
Government of India. In case the Government of India, Minis-
= of Home Affairs makes any amendment in the rules or issues
instructions to this Government, their cases can be taken up by
this Government, accordingly.”

[Government of Himachal Pradesh, Department of Personnel (A-I)

O.M. No. 8|171|76-DP (Apptt.) dated the 7th August, 1980].

ber of Extra Assistant Commissioners, who could not find place in
the initial constitution of the Himachal Pradesh Administrative _
Service, as given by the Minister of State in the Ministry of Home _
Affairs in his letter dated the 26th May, 1980, and as mentioned by
Shri K. N. Dhulap in his note dated the 19th January, 1979, has been
reconciled, हू

50. The Committee also notes that in accordance with its recom-
mendation for the removal of the grievences of the aggrieved officers,
the Himachal Pradesh Government have amended the Himachal
Pradesh Administrative Service/Himachal Pradesh Police Service



27

negligence on the part of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Com-
mittee reiterates its earlier recommendation that in future the
Ministry of Home Affairs should always take adequate and necessary
measures to sefeguard the interests of the employees.

MEMORANDUM 
SuBJECT: Sixty-Fourth Raport of the Public Accounts Committee 
(Fourth Lok Sabha)~Statutory Control over Govern­
ment's borrowing 
The Public Accounts Committee in para 1.11 of their Sixty­
Fourth Report have made the following recommendation:-
"The Committee have carefully 1considered the arguments put 
forward by Government for not accepting their repeated 
suggestion that a practical trial should be given to the 
healthy principle enunciated in Article 292 of the Cons­
titution for fixing a Limit by Parliament on Public 
borrowings. ·The country is now committed to planning 
on a five-years basis. This necessary presupposes a 
long-term assessment of resources needed for develop­
mental effort and the extent to whkh such resources 
should be raised through additional taxation 
borrowing and deficit financing. It should, there­
fore, be possible to vvork out with a reasonable degree of 
approximation a workable limit on borrowings for pur­
pose of incorporation in a statute as contemplated in 
Article 292 of the Constitution. The Committee would 
like Government to reconsider their position in the light 
of the foregoing considerations. 
2. The reasons for which the Government found it difficult tc. 
accept the earlier recommendations of the Public Accounts Commit­
tee had been explained in the Memorandum dated 29th January, 
27 

1967 submitted to the 
below:~ 
28 
Committee. These are briefly recounted 
"(i) The constitutional provision regarding Government's 
borrowings is permissive and not mandatory (Article 
292). 
(ii) Broad limits of the net borrowing proposed over a Plan 
periorl through domestic market loans from Reserve 
Bank, and through Budgetary receipts corresponding to 
external assistance . are generally indicated in the Plan 
documents. 
(iii) The borrowings proposed during the ensuing financial 
year by various categori>es are shown distinctly in the 
Budget presented to Parliament. 
The budget documents, of course, do not indicate the timing a;; 
well as the terms and conditions of the proposed borrow­
ings nor would it be possible to do so even if there is to 
be any statutory provision in regard to limits, etc. 
(iv) :Parliament has ample opportunity to discuss the pro­
posed borrowings by Government (a) over a plan period 
and (b) also during this ensuing financial year when it 
discusses the plan and the annual Budget. Moreover, in 
the ultimate analysis Government's borrowings from all 
sources are limited by the supply gr~nted by Parliament, 
the re~uirements for which cannot be raised through 
sources like Revenue etc. 
(v) Limits on borrowings from Reserve Bank present. special 
problem. These vary not only from year to year but even 
from time to time during· a year itself, 8Jccording to cir­
cumstances, needs and other considerations. It is only 
the net borrowing over a year which is of significance 
but any enactment in regard to limits would have to be 
with reference to the maximum amount of borrowing at 
any time and not the net over the year and this would be 
misleading. 
(vi) Limits on external borrowings would be even more 
difficult. The extent of such borrowings depends on the 
prevailing circumstances and involve p~tient negotiat:io~s. 
It would not be desirable or even practicable to put hm1tls 
on such borrowings halving regard to the factors which 
affect external assistance. 

, .. 
• 29 
(vii) If borrowirigs from. Reserve Bank and foreign loans are 
left out, any legislative approval for the residuary borrow~ 
ings will have little significance. 
(viii) If notwithstanding the foregoing consideration sta­
tutory limits. are though necessary, these would have to 
be sufficiently wide so that the need for frequent amend·· 
~·· ments to the statute does not arise. On the other hand, 
such wide limits:-which are by and large already set by 
the Plan documents and the annual Budgets-will serve 
no practical purpose. Statutory limits would, therefore, 
confer no advantage but on the other hand hamper the 
flexibility which is now available: 
3. In their latest recommendation contained in para 1.11 of the 
Sixty-Fourth Report (Fourth Lok Sabha), the Public Accounts 
Committee have suggested that a workable limit on borrowings can 
be incorporated in a st~atute in the light of the assessment of re­
sources made for the purpose of Five Year Plan. The assessment of 
resources made in the Five Year Plan is based on certain assump­
tions and is apt to be affected by development not foreseeable at the 
time of formulation of the Plan. For example, there ' were wide 
Yvariations between the scheme of financJng contemplated in the 
Third Plan and the actuals. The assumptions made in the Five 
Year Plans cannot, therefore, be taken as firm basis for fixing sta~ 
tutory limits on borrowings. The Five Year Plan is reviewed 
annually and the annual Plan and the annual Budget reflect the 
latest estimates for the year in regard to the debt to be incurred 
under various heads. But these too are subject to fluctuations. 
4. Parliament is Kept fully apprised of tihe borrowing of the 
Government. In fact, the Budget documents show not only the 
details of the borrowing programme for the Budget Year by cate­
gories, but also of the growth of Public Debt ever since 1950-51 vide 
Statement VI in Section II of Part II of tihe Explanatory Memo­
randum on the Budget. Moreover, in the ultimate analysis, Govern­
ment's borrowings are even now limited indirectly by the Parlia­
ment, year to year, by setting limits to the total expenditure to be 
incurred by the Government. 
/ 5. In view of the reasons stated above 9overnment even after 
~~reconsidering the matter .are of the view that no real advan.tage 
will ,be served by. prescribing statutory limits on Government 
borrowings,

The other point raised by the Committee relates to the pro­

Prescribed Officer/Bank. We presume the reference has been made 
to the provisions of rule 21 (2) of .the 1975 Rules. It may be point­
ed out in this connection that this rule is merely in the nature of a

clear that the Prescribed Officer's or the Bank's decision in respect 
of a claim made under the 1975 Rules shall be final. It is necessary 
to retain this rule specially in the light of subsequent delegation, to· 
the public sector banks. It may be stated . that in terms of sub­
rule (2) of this Rule even though no appeal against the decision 
of the Prescribed Officer /Bank in regard to any claim therein shall 
lie the Prescribed Officer himself or the Bank itself is not precluded , . 
from reviewing its decision. The Bank has in this connection 
iSsued administrative instructions that if the Prescribed Officer (or

the question whether the decision of ihe Prescribed Officer is objec­

of statute; there is no inherent right of appeal''.

"The undersigned is directed to ~te that during the course of

of the Committee generally felt concerned about this restriction 
which barred entry of even a citizen of India to the Islands which

authorising the Government to impose. such a restridion. The

mittee's notice the provision of the Rules made unde:c sub-section

(Laws) Regulations, 1965, made by the President in exercise of the

(1) Point referred:

These rules have been made under the Children Act, 1960 after
a lapse of 12 years. The reasons for this inordinate delay in
framing the rules may be explained.

Ministry’s comments:

The Children Act, 1960, was enforced in this Territory in 1964.
However, a Regular Probation Officer was appointed only in
1970. The Rules were framed thereafter in 1972 based on the
Rules framed by Delhi Administration. This took time.

(2) Point referred:

‘he regular probation Officer was appointed in the year 1970
and rules were framed in the year 1972. What are the reasons for
delay in the appointment of regular Probation Officer and the
framing of the rules.

Ministry’s comments:

With regard to the delay in the appointment of Regular Proba-
tion Officer and framing of the Rules, it may be mentioned that
the post of Probation Officer was created by the Goa Administra-

delay in this connection was due to the fact that information in
respect of similar recruitment rules in the neighbouring states
and Union Territories was to be collected as no such post was in
existence in Goa during that period. Further, after the framing
of the Recruitment Rules and their notification in the Govern-
ment Gazette, the post was advertised by the U.P.S.C. and filled
by a regular Probation Officer. This naturally took its own time.

India had foreseen the potential of atomic energy for power gene-

|. tation as far back as 1944, almost 40 years ago. At the end of the

Second World War, when most vf the nations viewed atomic energy

as a force of destruction, India was already thinking in terms of using
atomic energy solely for economic development.

Jt was late Dr. H. J. Bhabha who recognised, in those early days,
the important role that atomic energy could play in India’s develop-
ment, and initiated the nuclear programme in the country, :

Though the country had a long and rich tradition of research in
the sciences, organised studies in nuclear sciences may be said to have
begun with the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Bom-
bay, which was founded in June, 1945, by Dr. Bhabha.

In April, 1948, the Indian Legisiature passed the Atomic Energy
Act, 1948, for the developmeni and control of Atomic Energy and for
purposes connected therewith. To achieve the objectives, efforts were
initiated to build up a versatile infrastructure of research facilities,
trained scientifie and technical manpower, raw material processing
centres and the know-how and capability to manufacture nuclear
components and electronic equipment to support the atomic energy
Programme and make the couniry self-reliant.

With work in atomic energy growing, the TIFR group of nuclear
scientists and a major part of the work on atomic energy was moved
to Trombay, where a separate multi-disciplinary unit, named as the
Atomic Energy Establishment was set up in 1954. The Establish-
ment was formally inaugurated by the late Prime Minister Shri
Jawaharlal Nehru on January 20, 1954.

Thereafter in September, 1962, Parliament passed the Atomic
Energy Act, 1962 (in supersession of the 1948 Act), to provide for
the development, conduct and use of atomic energy for the welfare
of the people of India and for other peaceful purposes and for mat-
ters connected therewith.

In January 1967, the Atomic Energy Establishment was renamed
as Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) to perpetuate the me-
mory of Dr. Bhabha.

With a manpower strength of 11,000 including 3,000 scientists and
engineers, the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre is today one of the
largest and best equipped research Centres in the world. Over the
years, it has built strong research groups and a wide range of modern
facilities in a number of disciplines covering diverse fields of activi-
ties such as physics, chemistry, engineering, metallurgy, reprocess-
ing, fuel fabrication, waste management, radio isotopes, electronics,
instrumentation, biology, agriculture, food technology, radiation me-
dicine etc.

Thus, India has reached a stage where it has a sound infrastruc-
ture of industry and know-how io support and sustain all the re-
quired activities encompassing feasibility studies detailed project

Shri A. P. Bhatikar, Secretary of the Central Silk Board wel-
comed the Chairman and the Members of the Committee and intro-
duced the officers of the Board to the Committee.

Giving a brief introduction of the Board the Chairman told the
Committee that the Central Silk Board had been maintaining a
steady growth of about 7 per cent to 8 per cent per annum in the
production of silk during the past three years, India’s position in
the production of silk was third, the first and second being China
and Japan, respectively. The main reason why China and Japan
were above India in the production of silk was that the Cocoons
which they produced were of superior quality. Besides, they backed
by an experience of over 100 years. India was however trying to
improve the quality of Cocoons. Whereas India’s experience in
the line was practically 10 to 20 years.

Giving a brief introduction of the Board the Chairman told the
Committee that the Central Silk Board was set up in the year 1949
under the Central Silk Board Act, 1948. In the initial stages the
Board functioned primarily as an Advisory Body and also as an
Agency for distribution of grants and loans to the State Govern-
ments against approved schemes. It did not take up any direct
activity relating to development of sericulture industry. In the
year 1958, pursuant to a decision taken by the Govt. of India, the
Board was made responsible for organising sericultural research,
advanced training of personnel and basic seed production under its
direct control with the taking over of sericulture, Research and



‘Training institutions from State Governments, the activities of
the Board increased and consequently its Budget and Staff also
increased manifold. The Committee was told that the Seventh Five
Year Plan envisages an infrastructure of development plans. The
Board had realised its role in the field of marketing too and there
were plans to set up all India price stability Boards.

The Committee had discussions with the representatives of the
Board on the (1) The Central Silk Board Rules, 1955 (2) The Cen-
tral Silk Board Study Leave Rules (8) The Central Silk Board
Contributory Provident Fund Rules and (4) The Central Silk Board
(General Provident Fund) Rules, 1966, all framed under the Cen-
tral Silk Board Act, 1948. The Committee expressed its satisfac-
tion that the Ministry had acceded to many of the suggestions made
by it in respect of certain provisions of the above rules,

The representatives of the Board told that a Committee under
the Chairmanship of Dr. A, Kalanidhi was on the job of consolidating
the various Rules of the Board and that its report was expected
shortly,

As regard the Central Silk Board Recruitment Rules, the Sec-
retary of the Board said that a task force was on the job of con-
solidating the four sets of Recruitment Rules and its proceedings
were at the final stage.

The Chairman thanked the representatives of the Central Silk
Board for the valuable information/clarification given by them,
